common_name: China S-1 Satsuma (Hubei-Origin Cold-Hardy Satsuma Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost risk has passed; China S-1 descends from satsuma trees that survived a severe freeze in Hubei and Sichuan Provinces, China, and was brought into U.S. evaluation collections specifically for its combination of good cold hardiness with acceptable fruit quality and vigor.

directions: China S-1 is one of a numbered series of satsuma selections collected from Chinese orchards after a catastrophic freeze wiped out less hardy trees, chosen because the parent tree survived and kept producing decent fruit under conditions that killed neighboring satsumas. It has become a reference variety in cold-hardy citrus trial collections for comparing hardiness against Gulf Coast standards like Owari and Brown Select, offering solid, easy-peel, seedless mandarin fruit with slightly more modest eating quality than the top Gulf Coast selections but a meaningful edge in wood hardiness. Grow it as a hedge against a hard winter loss in a mixed satsuma planting rather than as your only tree, since its main strength is survival rather than superior flavor. Protect young trees for their first two winters and expect full hardiness benefits only once the tree is well established.
sources: University of California Riverside — Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
Auburn University cold-hardy citrus germplasm evaluations
Louisiana State University AgCenter — satsuma variety trial notes

common_name: China S-9 Satsuma (Smooth-Peel Hubei-Origin Cold-Hardy Satsuma Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost risk has passed; China S-9 comes from the same post-freeze Hubei Province survivor collection as China S-1 and is distinguished in variety trials by a notably smoother rind than most other satsuma selections.

directions: China S-9 was selected from the same freeze-survivor orchards in Hubei and Sichuan Provinces as other numbered China satsuma lines, prized by cold-hardy citrus collectors for pairing good winter hardiness with a smoother, glossier peel than typical satsumas, which some growers find easier to hand-peel. Fruit quality and vigor are rated acceptable rather than exceptional, placing it a notch below flagship Gulf Coast satsumas like Brown Select or Owari in eating quality, but its cold tolerance makes it a useful backup planting in the coldest parts of zone 8. Give it full sun and excellent drainage, and treat it as part of a diversified home citrus planting rather than a single specimen, since its selection criteria prioritized survival over peak flavor. As with other satsuma types, expect full production and best fruit quality only after the tree is several years established.
sources: University of California Riverside — Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
